newsitem.title: SPAIN: Dlr drags down peseta, and no help seen from home.
newsitem.headline: Dlr drags down peseta, and no help seen from home.

text.p: The peseta was punished on Monday by a weaker U.S. dollar and it will find little short-term relief given a heated domestic political debate and strong expectations of an official Spanish rate cut soon, dealers said.
"The U.S. dollar is responsible for at least 60 percent of the peseta's decline," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
At 1245 GMT, the peseta was trading at 84.63/64 versus the mark from an open at 84.65/68 and Friday's close of 84.56/58. It has weakened from levels near 84.20/40 in much of April.

If the U.S. dollar's recent tumble continues, the peseta could be pulled to trade around 84.80 per mark. But the Bank of Spain will not allow the peseta to trade lower than 85.0 per mark, a level it has staunchly defended in recent months, dealers said.
"If the dollar goes toward 1.67 per mark, the peseta could fall to 84.80," said Cesar Cantalapiedra, economist at Analistas Financieros Internacionales.
The Bank of Spain will, however, shrug off current foreign exchange market pressure in setting its policy, focusing on inflation unless the peseta breached 85 per mark, economists said.

"The Spanish market is expecting good (April) CPI, and then a rate cut from the Bank of Spain. This has something to do with the peseta's weakness," said Carmen Hernansanz, economist of Merrill Lynch in Madrid.
April CPI, due on Wednesday, is expected to show a tame 1.9 percent year-on-year rate, which compares favourably with the 29-year low of 2.2 percent set in March.
And that should prompt the Bank of Spain to cut its official rate as soon as Friday's repurchase tender by 25 basis points to 5.25 percent, analysts said.

"If the peseta holds current levels, I do not think that the rate outlook will change," said Hernansanz, adding that only if the peseta were to fall to around 84.90/85.00 could that endanger a fresh rate cut.
A heated political brushfire was also undermining the peseta, although its effect was considered small.
"Political tensions are never good," said Urrutia, who said that factor was 10 percent of the reason behind the peseta's recent weakness.
In the last two weeks, the one-year-old conservative Popular Party government has been exchanging accusations with the opposition Socialist party.
Catalan and Basque leaders, who lend crucial support to the government, complained that the government had not completely kept initial promises made to them.
Although the market appeared to dislike the rumblings, it saw little imminent danger to the government and therefore reacted modestly.
"If the political conflict had an effect, it was a very modest one. I'd give more importance to the U.S. dollar weakness," said Hernansanz.
Longer-term, analysts remained bullish over peseta-denominated assets.
"I'm sure the peseta will continue to capitalise on the good rise in stocks and bonds and the latest European Union's positive assessment of Spain's convergence plan," said Cantalapiedra.
European Union finance ministers welcomed on Monday Spain's economic 1997-2000 convergence plan.
-- Madrid Newsroom, + 341 585 8340
